utterances.text: I went on playing by myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, at some stage, did you go near the wall in front of your house and do something with the flowers in the garden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen to you while you were near the wall in front of your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I was hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you were hit, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, I don't think anyone struck me with a stone. I was wounded from the side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's important that you tell us exactly what happened. When you say you were hit, you were hit with what? What were you hit with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: A sniper bullet. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At that instant when you were hit, what position were you in? Were you standing up or bending over or kneeling or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I was kneeling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you facing as you were kneeling when you were hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: My back was more or less to the wall, and my face towards a spikey rock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts -- withdraw that. Whereabouts were you shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In the area of my shoulder blade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the bullet stay in your body or did it pass through your body?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please turn off your microphone when listening to the answer, please. Yes. Please proceed, Miss E.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, the bullet went through my body and ended up in the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please, in a moment, slowly stand up and turn around and when I ask you to, point to where the bullet entered your body, and then, when I ask you to, point to where the bullet left your body.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I assume that if the witness does that slowly, the face distortion can be maintained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I just am looking to the technical booth, that they are prepared that the witness will stand up slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please, now, turn around and point to where the bullet entered your body, if you can reach that point with the fingers of -- one of your fingers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness indicates the back of the right shoulder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now point to the position where the bullet left your body.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Witness points to the same area but further down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please now sit down. Were you able to accurately indicate those positions, or were you constrained by the difficulty in touching that part of your body with your hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, because I was a small child, as I have already said, the scars moved, I suppose, as my body grew so I cannot reach the exact spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now what did you do after you were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I stood up and went to the house, sat on the threshold, and I called out to my mother and said that I had been hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive some treatment from your aunt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your aunt a nurse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: She is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then taken to a hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken from the house with the assistance of a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else took you from the house? And please, do not use names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: A friend whom I mentioned, who played with me. There was his father and another neighbour, and then we went to a third person who put me in his car and drove me away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen as you were being driven away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Fire was opened on the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, coming back to your position at the time that you were shot, you've told us that your back was facing towards a particular place. What was the name of that place that your back was facing towards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Do you mean the street?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. This is an intrusive question because it is quite contrary to what the witness said. I will quote line 51.12, where the witness said this: "More or less to the wall." [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not Mr. Ierace; it was quite the opposite. 51.12.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand the objection, Mr. President. And I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that when you were shot, I think you said that you were kneeling or squatting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were kneeling or squatting, which direction were you facing? Were you facing towards the house, to the side of the house, or away from the house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please turn off the microphone. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same objection. The witness has already answered this question clearly, and the Prosecutor is saying opposite. The witness has already said that she had her back to the wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer was that the back was more or less to the wall, so I would allow some questions which will not deny the answer given, that it was more or less to the wall. Especially when someone is kneeling, it might not be clear, right on. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll approach it a different way. Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, in relation to your position, a spiky rock. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Does Mr. Ierace could quote the line so that we can follow him in the transcript, please [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's also in my recollection that the rock was mentioned. But, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it's the same page and line reference that my learned colleague gave. It's page 51, at line 10 is the question: "Where were you facing as you were kneeling when you were hit?" Answer: "My back was more or less to the wall, and my face towards a spiky rock."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "a spiky rock"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Probably what I meant was probably that's where the bullet had come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: You mean where the bullet came from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, where you say the bullet came from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It's called Spicasta Stijena, sharp rock feature, or a spiky rock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is that -- I think that's sometimes known as Sharpstone in English. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown two photographs which are Exhibit P3273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Usher, could you assist Mr. Ierace in giving the photographs to the witness. How about the ELMO and protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are no signatures or other -- certainly no signatures on the photographs. As to the appearance of the various features in the photographs -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would ask that the photographs not be disclosed publicly. I don't know if it's possible for the images on the ELMO not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd just wait for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nothing that's on the ELMO will be shown to the outside world until I give further orders that they can resume the normal manipulation of the pictures. You may put the picture on the ELMO, or just in front of the witness, but I think on the ELMO would be better. Mr. Usher, would you please turn the ELMO in the direction of the witness so that she can see what's on the ELMO, and please put the... Yes, please put it on the ELMO. Could you please guide the usher in what photograph should be first put on the ELMO, Mr. Ierace. Would that be the photograph with the number 4288 at the end, which is marked with a letter B?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make a statement to an investigator from the Prosecutor's office on the 26th of September -- excuse me -- 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you made the statement, were you shown the photograph which is on the screen on your -- withdraw that. The photograph which is on your right under the mirror?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have two photographs in front of you; one shows a house, and the other shows a yard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the photograph which shows the house, did you take a black pen and put some marks on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose house is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: My parents' house, my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You placed some marks over a balcony and a room underneath the balcony. Was the balcony and the room underneath it there on the day that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, they weren't. This was done later. This was built later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that just before you were shot, you had been playing. Can you see in this photograph the area where you had been playing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: You mean to show you on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the photograph show you the area where you were playing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that area in relation to the room beneath the balcony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you're pointing to an area just to the left of the room as one looks at the photograph. Is that correct? Is that where you were playing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Not quite. Not quite left of the room. The room is inside, but it is just as you go in from the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean by that that you were playing in the area which, in the photograph, has a room on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Will you now please look at the other photograph, that is, the one that ends with the number 4289. At the time that you made your statement in September 2001, did you also place some marks on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the photograph show?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The actual place from where the shot was fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But leaving aside the marks that you placed on the photograph, and looking at the bottom of the photograph, you can see some grass and a tree. Whereabouts was that grass and the tree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They were in the same place, but it was much smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the same place as the yard which appears in the first photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this, in fact, a photograph looking in the other direction, that is, away from the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see in this photograph anywhere the area that you earlier referred to as a spiky rock?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indicate that area with an arrow when you put some marks on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The tree which is growing in the grass, was that as big on the day that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, it was smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the line in red ink that you drew through the tree indicate its approximate height at the time that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the red line that is drawn through the other tree indicate its approximate height, as well, on the day that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This is for the transcript, for the record. There are several red lines, and I believe Mr. Ierace has just spoken about another red line. So it seems that it would be good enough for the record to say which red line exactly we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the first question was about the tree growing in the grass. That explains one line. And then the next question was about the red line that is drawn through the other tree, so I do not see what misunderstanding there could be as a matter of fact. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you were shot and you were kneeling, were you facing towards the spiky rock?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had your back to the house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is the same objection as a moment ago. I'll going to rephrase it. The back was to the house more or less --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I have had time to rethink it. If you would been on your knees kneeling, then it very often happens that the back is in a horizontal position, which could be at one end at the wall, but at another end be somewhere else. If the witness says more or less the back was to the wall, that doesn't mean that the back of a person kneeling is exclusively in one direction. So I deny your objection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more precise as to the position you were in at the instant that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I can repeat: I was -- my back was facing the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but can you tell us in what position your body was in terms of standing or kneeling or squatting or whatever.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I was kneeling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Why were you kneeling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Because I was playing with the flowers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know where the bullet went after it left Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, it hit the wall. It ended in the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it leave a mark in the wall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the bullet remained in the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was there anything near you when you were kneeling when you were shot? In other words, any part of the building or part -- or steps or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There were steps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the steps lead to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They were going by the house, so by the place where I was, going by the house, and then they were going to the street, towards the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage, if it's convenient, I'd like the video to be shown. As I indicated earlier, it has not yet been redacted, and therefore it would be appropriate for it to be shown in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then go into closed session, and Madam Registrar will tell us whenever we are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session again. May I have a confirmation that the face and voice distortion is still -- yes. I see that it is. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise yourself in the video that you just watched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The investigator asked you to point out a number of things. When you pointed them out, were you doing so truthfully and to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. Yes, according to my recollection, the way I remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you kneeling on at the time you were shot? Was it dirt or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Steps. There were steps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some stage, although we don't see it on the video, did you see the investigator appear to measure a distance from where you had told him you were kneeling at the time that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. They measured, but I don't know what they were measuring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on other days, days before this happened, had you seen people walking through that yard where you were playing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I was watching it right from the beginning of 1992 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sometimes see soldiers go through that yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, but not in an organised manner, not in any way convoys. They were just walking individually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen anyone travel through that yard on the morning that you were shot before you were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Before I went out, that's when I saw it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I saw civilians, children, everybody passed through there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the morning before you went out to play, you said that you saw something. Did you see any people passing through the yard before you went out to play that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see that morning before you went out to play passing through the yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There may have been a couple of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone pass through the yard while you were outside playing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you playing for before you were shot approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Perhaps an hour, hour and a half, maybe two. But certainly an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you realised before that day that it was possible to see the spiky rock from that yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, but only a small portion of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever been shot at before that day while you were in that same yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Not on that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown again Exhibit P3273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, if before we do so, this would be a suitable moment to have our next break, then perhaps we show the photo to the witness after the break. Miss E, we'll have a break for 20 minutes. We'll then resume, and I hope we'll have not the same technical problems as we had before for which I apologise. It's drawing our attention on things that are not the most important things in this courtroom. Mr. Ierace, may I invite you to inform the Court after the break about the issue we raised just at the beginning of this session about the 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. We'll then have a break until 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before resuming, Mr. Ierace, I would like to make a remark first, and that's a remark concerning the interpretation. We seriously have considered, in order to assist the interpreters, to go into closed session, which would solve their problem. Finally, we decided not to do so. We have great admiration for the way the interpreters, under these difficult circumstances, are performing their task. I would like to stress that and to emphasise that. On the other hand, as we all know, the public character of the trial is of such importance that it is prevailing in our view. And therefore, with full understanding from the difficulties the interpreters are facing at this moment and with great admiration with how they are performing their task, we nevertheless decided we would stay in open session. Then perhaps before I give an opportunity to you, Mr. Ierace, to make any remarks. General Galic, I'm informed that the detention unit is, at this moment, trying to make arrangements for tomorrow in the afternoon. If that would not be possible, then it might Thursday morning, but everyone is working on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you please briefly inform the Chamber. And in order to avoid whatever misunderstanding, this Chamber is not of the view that 92 bis witnesses could not be heard in The Hague, but the Chamber is of the opinion that if there would be any need for cross-examination of the witness, then we would better use the presence of the witness. That's the only reason why I made the remark. Please make whatever observations you'd like to make in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand that that is the issue, Mr. President. I've made some inquiries. There were two witnesses travelling to The Hague this week in order to go through the 92 bis procedure. The first of those was Oystein Strand who was an officer of the Royal Norwegian Air Force. He arrived yesterday and is due to leave tonight. It's too late for us to do anything in relation to him, as I understand it. In fact, I have been recently told that he has left. The second witness, Mr. Karel Lindr from the Czeck Republic is due to arrive tomorrow at 3.00, and we are making efforts to try to change the travel arrangements so that he comes at a later date. The reason is, we already have sufficient witnesses this week to give evidence in The Hague from Sarajevo, and we are working under some difficulty because of Bajram to finish them so that they can return to Sarajevo by Friday morning at the very latest. So, Mr. President, that's why we are attempting to forestall the arrival of Mr. Lindr so that we can take advantage of the Trial Chamber's proposal at a later date. Mr. President, two other matters, the first is related to that issue: If it transpires that General Galic receives medical treatment on Thursday morning, and if it also transpires that we will not be sitting for all or a part of Thursday morning, I would be grateful it we could have some forewarning of that. Again, so as to assist the Sarajevoian witnesses to return in time for Bajram. If it transpires that one of those witnesses is in the witness box, but has not finished their testimony, then I would propose that subject to the requirements of the Victims and Witness Unit, we take all possible to allow that witness to return to Sarajevo, and then come back at a later date to finish their evidence. The third matter, Mr. President, just very briefly, in relation to the software for your computers so that you can view the 360-degree photographs, steps have been taken to make that software available. I'm told that the most efficient way of doing it is to load it directly on to your computers, and that would be done by technicians of the OTP. I anticipate that that can probably be done by Thursday afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the floor. So we see that the problem is not a simple one; it is a double problem, that is two witnesses and not one witness affected by 92 bis, and it surprises us all the more so because these persons are people who were on UN mission there, and who are therefore of major importance for the Defence. In a nutshell, the Defence, in principle, does not accept that such statements be done in a manner prescribed by 92 bis, and we most emphatically oppose such procedure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware from your submissions that you are opposing mainly the 92 bis. One of the issues I had, first of all, whenever Mr. Lindr come, perhaps a later date, could there be some kind of arrangement that the Defence is informed prior to giving a statement outside this courtroom and immediately provided with a statement so that if, for example, he would stay for another half a day or a day, that if good cause is shown why he should be cross-examined, that we could give a decision right away and then perhaps call Mr. Lindr at that very moment. One of the things, at least that is of some consolation to me, is that both witnesses are able to travel on their own and not need the assistance of the Victims and Witnesses Unit. At least they are not escorted by the Registry to and from The Hague. There's another issue I'd like to draw the attention to from the Defence. If it would turn out that General Galic would be examined physically on Thursday morning, would the Defence consider -- of course, dependent on where we are with the witness that is examined at that very moment, whether we could finish or not even without the presence of General Galic, and if there would come a point where the Defence would say, well, this is specifically a point on which we would have to consult our client, would you please consider it? Perhaps it might not be necessary at all if it could be dealt with on Wednesday in the afternoon, there would be no problem at all. But if, for example, you would have half an hour remaining for one of the witnesses or -- would you please consider what to do under these circumstances if it would turn out to be necessary to have General Galic be examined on Thursday morning. I will not in whatever way infringe upon any right to be present during the trial. So it's not urging you, but just to consider it, depending on the circumstances. Then I see you nodding, so I...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe, Mr. President, we shall perhaps try to see with what you have told us, we shall try to inform the Chamber as soon as possible. I believe that in principle, there will be no difficulty because it could be obviously a very short interruption. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have in mind that we should be able to stick to the seven-day rule in relation to Mr. Lindr. In relation to his statements, I informed the Defence in writing late last year that we intended to seek to convey the evidence of Mr. Lindr and also Mr. Strand by way of 92 bis, so I'm sure that's not a surprise to my friend. And the statements have also already been served, but, of course, we will treat them in the usual fashion so there will be seven days' notice of when that will be here. Excuse me, Mr. President. I've just been informed that it's not possible at this late stage to cancel Mr. Lindr's travel arrangements. We have attempted in the last hour to do that so that becomes academic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we will see when he returns, if there's good cause shown that he should be cross-examined, he'll have to return. We'll decide on that. If on Thursday morning we have any extra time, I indicated to you before that an oral hearing, I think it was especially the 92 bis, could take place at any suitable moment when there are no witnesses. So would you please, as I asked you before, be prepared to have oral arguments on the 92 bis issue, and I think it would be proper to provide the Chamber, then, with the 92 bis statements that you intend to use in Court because several of the criteria of 92 bis require the Chamber to have a look in the statements as such. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence apologises in advance for what I'm about to say, but bearing in mind the duration of this case, as the lead counsel, I have asked to leave on Thursday morning, and I have been authorised to travel. On Thursday, if there are any witnesses, my distinguished co-counsel will be here, and then the trial will go on as it has started. But I would like to voice my wish to -- for us to be both present during the argument about Rule 92 bis. I thought I would notify you at the end of today, because I should be leaving on Thursday morning. Now I understand that the argument about 92 bis could be on Thursday, and I would dearly like, if possible, to schedule it for some other day when both Mr. Piletta-Zanin and I are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll keep that in mind, and we'll give full consideration to the wish you just expressed. If you would come up with any suggestion how to use our time then on Thursday as good as we can, I gave you to consider, even to continue, even when General Galic would not be present, although I'm hesitant to do so. But just consider what you could do in order not to waste any time. I think that's what we all try to do in this courtroom, and I'm really convinced that you'll assist us as good as you can. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the 92 bis statements are taken in the Bosnian language. We are taking steps to obtain translations. In the most part, the original statement will suffice, but in a few cases where there is some additional information, I at least anticipate that I will have an informal translation of at least those additional parts available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's wise, Mr. Ierace, since Ms. Pilipovic will not be present and would like to attend the oral argument, and since you are not fully prepared yet as far as the translation is concerned that we just take our time and do it somewhere next week or the week afterwards in order not to fall into any sloppy performance of what we have to do in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. President, I anticipate that the witnesses we have lined up will take us to Thursday afternoon at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we use our time in that way. Ms. Pilipovic, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we then could resume the examination of Witness E. Mr. Usher, could you please bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will take the witness to the 360-degree photograph. And for the same reason, may that photograph not be displayed publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We did not give any order in respect of any pictures of -- put on the ELMO to be broadcasted to the outside world. Could I ask the assistance of the technical booth that the computer evidence which will now be shown by the case manager of the Prosecution will not be broadcasted out of this courtroom. Yes. This being the case, Mr. Ierace, when the witness is brought in, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. I have to notify the Chamber that we have just talked with General Galic and he says that he would like to be present in the courtroom at all times when the witness testimonies go on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have full respect for this position taken by General Galic. So we'll not continue in his absence. Miss E, you had to wait even some 20 more minutes since we had not only technical problems, but also some legal technical issues we had to discuss. Please be seated. And Mr. Ierace will now resume the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the 360-degree photograph be displayed. As always, I think the best picture is on the "computer evidence" button.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the view which appears on your monitor at the moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I have nothing before me. It's okay. It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was whether you recognised what you see on the screen at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that appear to be a view of the yard in front of your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think we can also see another house which has a white wall in front of that yard. Is that correct? In front of your front yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please manoeuvre the picture to the right slowly. Pause for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we see now the doorway and the door of the addition to the front of your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue to pan the picture. Please pause.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we now see the wall of the house, that is, it is now an internal wall of the addition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see on the wall of the house the yellow paint marks that were made by the investigator, as seen on the video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The yellow circle indicates the approximate position that the bullet hit the wall. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The yellow line underneath it indicates the height of the steps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the yellow line at the bottom indicates the ground level on the day that you were shot. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue to pan the photograph to the right. Please pause.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when people travelled through your yard, did they come from the view that we see on the screen at the moment, which is towards the left from the doorway of the addition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue to pan the photograph. Please pause.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we are now back where we started; that is, looking at the front yard from the doorway of the addition. Having regard to the photographs that you have already seen in this courtroom, do we see, between the roofs of the two houses, towards the centre of the photograph, the area known as - and please pardon my pronunciation - Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the photograph could be zoomed in on that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we now see that area zoomed in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that -- on the date that you were shot, the armed conflict was taking place in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, there was no conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not so much speaking about that particular day, but that was one of the years during which there was fighting around Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Spicasta Stijena appears to be, from the photograph, a ridge at least. On which side of the confrontation line was the ridge, that is, the very top of the ridge that one can see in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand that the two armies, the two principal armies that were involved in the conflict were the army for the Bosnian government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must object because once he speaks of the two chief armies, and we know there were several, and this is a purely subjective opinion that there were two principal armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, not once in the now months of evidence has the Defence challenged the evidence of a very large number of witnesses to the effect that there were two principal armies involved. Not once has that been done, even though it's required, if this is the position of the Defence if they do so, by Rule 90. I am surprised to hear that, against that background, it is still an issue, particularly when one considers the content of the Defence pre-trial brief which is precisely to the same effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please respond to that, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It is quite true that, in general, we admit that there were two more important armies, and yet there are times -- there were times when the Croat forces were more better structured than the Bosnian forces, generally speaking, and to say simply which army or which armies, that is all why it can be said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is my recollection that there has been a considerable number of questions put to witnesses in order to find out where the confrontation lines were, but there was no question about whether there were three armies or four or five or six at the confrontation line. Is there any specific reason -- I mean, also it might not be that difficult to rephrase the question. And I could even order the Prosecution to do so. And I'm quite willing to do it, but on the other hand, of course, it comes into my mind what actually is at this moment the relevance of I would say importing a third, fourth, or fifth party to this question? But perhaps, Mr. Ierace, since I do not see that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is giving -- apart from that, I must say that, during the last couple of days, a third party has been introduced in the objections one or two times. So if you could rephrase the question, and if Mr. Piletta-Zanin, sustaining the objection, would consider next time the importance of his objection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fact, if my friend checks my question at page 76, line 7, he will see that the wording was: "The two principal armies." I therefore fail to understand the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you still persist by your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must say yes, but to say yes, I must discover their position. If you authorise me to do so, I will do that. For instance -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think we are wasting a lot of time on an issue which could be easily solved without a lot of explanations. I'll put one or two questions to the witness at this very moment. Miss E, you know sometimes there are some legal technical issues as well. You have referred to the rock you mentioned before. Do you know if this rock was under the control of an army at the time of the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what army that was or how you would refer to that army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that when you were being driven to hospital, that the car came under fire. Was the car actually hit by any bullets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of the car?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The back of the car was hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that the car was hit, how long had it been moving approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Under a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that the car was hit, if you had turned around and looked out the rear window, would it have been possible to see Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. And very clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the armed conflict, did any shells land in the vicinity of your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the year 1993, did any shells land in the vicinity of your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During 1993 did any shells hit your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many times during the conflict was your house hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Three times, three or four times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times -- withdraw that. When was the first time that a shell hit your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In early 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it hit again in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In 1993, twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your father in the army during the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your mother in the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any brothers or sisters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, a sister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she in the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any military equipment in your house during the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day, indeed at the time that you were shot, was there anyone else at all in the yard apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In the yard, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown Exhibit P1025. Mr. President, that document has the witness's signature on it, I anticipate. So perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if it's not necessary to put it on the ELMO, we would rather leave it at this moment, although there is still the order that nothing from the ELMO and also from the computer evidence will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a medical report in relation to the treatment that you received as a result of being shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might that be returned, and I ask the witness be shown Exhibit P3243. I don't require that to be placed on the ELMO either, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, it has been protected, the document, as well, if it would finally end up on the ELMO. Will there be any other documents to be tendered because we could then put it on the ELMO since it has been prepared for not showing the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: This is the last document. I don't require it to be put on the ELMO, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we rather not do it at this moment. Mr. Usher, would you please give it to the witness and not put it on the ELMO. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make a statement to the investigators in June 2001, that is, last year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you made your statement, did you place some marks with a red pen on a map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then sign the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you place a cross on the map to indicate approximately the position of your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you place some crossed lines on the map to indicate the approximate position of Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you place the number 2 in a circle alongside that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that completes examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Before I'll ask the Defence whether they are prepared for the cross-examination of the witness, I'd like to have one intermediary question at this very moment. Miss E, you told you this Spicasta Stijena was probably under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. You said "probably." What made you believe that it was probably under the control of the army of the Republika Srpska? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably because it isn't very far from the house to the Spicasta Stijena, it is easy to make this conclusion. When provocation start, there would be shouting, there would be swearing, cursing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean that you could hear from your house shouting from that specific place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how could you identify who was shouting, or could you tell us the words that were shouted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would be swear words mostly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how could you know exactly against whom these words were? Could you just give us one or two examples, then? It might be easier to understand for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For instance, during the -- if it was raining, many of them -- many people were using the rain water for water. So I'm sorry for the words that I'm going to use, so what they would say is balijas, trying and catch the rain. You will need it to wash your ass."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear. Thank you very much. Ms. Pilipovic, or Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. I thank you for being here. If this is the case, could you confirm that you did give a statement on the 27th of June, 2001 here in The Hague, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'm going to return to the facts, but before that I would like to ask the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we seem to be facing a new problem, which is to do with Rule 91 of the rules. I believe that this Rule is giving the Defence the opportunity to ask the Chamber to tell the witness -- to remind the witness of the necessity to speak the truth. I don't know whether this is necessary in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just give me one second, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're referring to Rule 91(A). As far as I can see, could you please start your cross-examination up until a moment where -- or if you indicated already during the examination-in-chief there are serious reasons to give a warning as referred to in 91(A), please tell the Court so that we can...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Simply because there are certain -- there's a testimony which was given today which isn't consistent with the written testimony of another day. So basically on this principle, I think that it is up to the Chamber to see whether this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll do it in the following way: Miss E, the counsel for the Defence has indicated that he has found contradictions between what you said before, giving a statement, and what your answers were on the questions put to you today by the Prosecutor. You well understand that if you say today this is what the truth is, then you're doing the right thing. If you say, no, what was -- I might have forgotten something or what I said earlier was the truth, then just inform this Chamber. I'm just stressing to you that it's of vital importance that whenever you have any doubt or whenever you don't remember anything, please tell us. And if you give your testimony to the best of your recollection, and in conformity with the solemn declaration you gave. I have not seen any of your earlier statements, so I do not know whether Mr. Piletta-Zanin is right in assuming that there are contradictions. But just answer to the best of your recollection whatever questions put to you by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, and that's what we expect you to do. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This was done in a very objective way, and I thank you for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said in line 10, to be precise, of page 61, that the bullet which went through your body remained in the wall. You declared this, and this is what I am quoting from the English transcript. Do you confirm this, what you said today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. The bullet remained in the wall. But when we returned, it had probably fallen out of the wall, so we couldn't establish exactly which bullet it was because there were several bullets. There were many bullets on the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because, Witness, I believe that you said at the time that the bullet did not remain in the wall, but it had ricochetted, and I'm talking about your written statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to have to read. I'm going to have to read, if you authorise me, according to the procedure that we have already had before part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you provide the statement to the interpreters' booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I here have a statement in English that I can read, and then the interpreters can interpret it so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please read.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The line says the following, and I'm going to read it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Miss E, Mr. Piletta-Zanin is now reading in the exact wording as it is written down in your statement given before to the investigators. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have before me the English transcript, which says the following, and I am quoting: "We didn't keep the bullet which had hit me. It wasn't in the wall, so it must have ricochetted off and fallen somewhere." [Interpretation] End of quote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'll just ask you a question. If you said that this bullet had ricochetted and when went off somewhere, and you said no. So could you perhaps explain what seems to the Defence to be a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: So I'm going to tell you what happened. The bullet hit the wall, and it stayed in the wall. But when we returned, it wasn't completely in the wall, not fully. It was not a deep hole in the wall. It fell out. And because of previous firing, there was shrapnel, there were bullets, there were all kinds of things on the floor. So where did not know which one of the bullets had been the one. But the bullet had hit the wall, and then fell out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I understand that it had fallen out, but it had not ricochetted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, it didn't ricochet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for specifying this. How can you be absolutely certain if there were several hits, bullets, that this was the one in question, that this was the bullet in question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, there were traces from bullets on all the wall, but not at the lower half of the house. This bullet that we saw was the first time we saw it then. In fact, I saw it straight away because it was very low. It was very low on that wall of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I believe you said -- I think I heard you say in your own language that there were -- there were several bullet cases on the floor, and shrapnel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps my learned colleague could take us to the passage where this witness said there were several bullet cases on the floor and shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I read in the English translation, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is that "... And because of previous firing, there was shrapnel, there were bullets, there were all kinds of things on the floor." Of course, it can be a matter of translation, whether there were any cases on the floor. Could I just ask the interpreters whether any of the interpreters heard the word "bullet cases"? I do not get a positive answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. I was listening to the -- so please, then, proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The answer was yes from the French booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, since there were bullets cases on the floor, so there was firing from that spot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I appreciate that you have been told by the French booth that they heard the word "cases." It doesn't appear in the English translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it's clear that this is a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I simply ask that it be clarified with the witness before my friend presumes that is the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you first seek confirmation of the answer given by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask my question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what I heard, I believe that you said, that you spoke -- that there were bits from bullets. Is that correct? And you spoke of --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There were bullets and there was shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this specification, Witness. I'm going to return to the military question. So you were not able to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for rising to my feet again. This is a very important issue. My friend has put to the witness that there were bullet cases. And that indicates that the bullets were fired from the spot. And I asked him, out of fairness, to clarify that, and he has not done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Miss E, you told us there were a lot of things on the ground. Were there bullet cases on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there were not bullet cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then please tell us exactly what was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shrapnel from the shells that had landed around the house before, and casings that were falling on the roof. They were shells. These are leftovers from bullets. You could see it all over during the war, everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did I understand you well, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you wanted to cover a new subject now. Because it's 10 minutes to 7.00, and if this would be a suitable moment to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can perfectly stop here if the Chamber authorise me and I can continue tomorrow with the witness. How long are we allowed to stay here, is it 7.00 or quarter to 7.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm mistaken. We can go on until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Had an early break today. That's my normal sense of time seems to be lost. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm continuing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for the clarifications. You said that your father was in the Territorial Defence. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father have a rank in his military unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the evidence was that her father was in the army. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that is what was my recollection as well. Was your father in the army or in the Territorial Defence, Miss E, or is it the same to you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all the same, everyone was in the army at the beginning of the war. Everything was called Territorial Defence, and then a couple of months later it was all called BH army. So he was just like the others. And I would like both parties -- I don't want any questions asked about the army because I'm not going to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is certainly taking the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll give the opportunity now to Mr. Piletta-Zanin to continue the cross-examination, and we'll see what happens. But as a general rule, you have to answer the questions. And whether there's any difficulty, just let me know because you're addressing the parties now. Just let me know and I'll try to solve whatever problem there might be. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you just said that you did not want to answer questions to do with the armies. What is the reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I don't allow any questions on this issue at this very moment. Please put the questions you have to do to the witness -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you did not answer to my previous question. You said did your father have a rank in his military organisation, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, you just said that for you, the Territorial Defence was the same thing as the army. Could you please clarify this or give more precision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: For this reason; because they were all on the same side. They were all fighting for one thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in one and in the other, in both entities, the Territorial Defence and the army, the soldiers or the members of the Defence, did they have regular uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would ask that the question be specific as to the year, since we've all heard evidence in the Trial Chamber that the situation varied from year to year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Miss E, may I just ask you, you just answered a question about uniforms. Could you tell us perhaps in more detail. Could you see any distinction between BiH army soldiers or military people and Territorial Defence people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- not I think but I know that. In the war, the uniforms were camouflage, all the same that the whole world has. They all looked the same. Some had green, some had blue. I was a child. How do I know who was wearing what? The civilians were wearing camouflage clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly the answer. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said yourself that at the time of the incident, that is, in [redacted] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think we did not refer to the date of -- and Madam Registrar, could you please make a redaction in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at the moment, at the time of the incident that you know the date of, you said that you were wearing a jacket which was blue. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Dark blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Which colour were the uniforms that we were speaking a moment ago in opposition to the other uniforms that we were calling camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There were all kinds of colours. If I -- you mean if I had been a soldier, a child of a few years of age with long hair?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I am not saying anything; I'm just asking a question. If you can answer, please answer; if you cannot answer, then do not answer. Things are very simple.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... please address me, and I'll see how we'll solve the problem. Yes, just be confident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin was whether you know about the colours of the uniforms the military people were wearing. And I felt from your answer that you feel a bit, perhaps, attacked, because your answer says that more or less would you compare a small child with a soldier, a small child with long hair, a girl. I fully understand your reaction, but if you could tell us what the colour of the uniforms was, I can assure you that this Court is perfectly well in a position to assess whether the colour you will mention could have created whatever confusion. We'll have to assess that at a later stage. But could you answer the question what the colours were of the military camouflage uniforms, uniforms you just described.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blue, green, yellow, white camouflage; all these colours. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this answer. The colour blue that you had is one thing, and you said you were wearing jeans. So could I ask you to tell us what was the colour of the trousers that you were wearing at the time of the incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Blue; navy blue, dark blue. It was a dark colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, to the best of your recollection, do you think that the top and the bottom of what you were wearing were, in a sense, a set?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two blues were completely different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to continue but perhaps, Mr. President, this is a good time for break. As you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think this is a good time to adjourn. Miss E, we'll continue tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. And don't worry, we'll find a way for you to answer the questions put to you. Whenever there's any difficulty, we'll find a solution for that. I hope you're confident that we'll achieve this. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, again my friend has misrepresented the evidence. He said that the witness had earlier stated she was wearing jeans. The relevant page and line is page 49, line 6, where he said she was wearing dark trousers and a blue jacket. But perhaps we could take that further tomorrow morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps before we adjourn, could the usher lead the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, Mr. Ierace, I experienced a lot of procedural incidents of which I thought not all of them to be necessary. I urge the parties to always consider fully what is the aim of these procedural incidents, whether they will serve the interest of the party in the best way since I have the feeling now and then that it causes more interventions from my side than I would wish to make. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
